title: Onboarding & Installfest (Welcome Aboard, Prep Machine + CLI, Interacting with Assignments)
summary: Day 1 turns your Mac into a developer machine: terminal basics, Homebrew, Python, Node, Git, the GitHub CLI, PostgreSQL, Docker and VS Code. It ends with the fork, clone, commit, push loop you use for every assignment.
goal: Run Python, JavaScript and SQL from your terminal, and fork, clone, commit and push a Code Platoon assignment.
required: Installfest assignment: CLI Practice (the Terminal Tutor course, then the local test/ folder exercise)
Installfest goal (TLO): run Python, JS and SQL programs from the command line and install dependencies with pip and npm
Installfest goal (TLO): write and edit code with VS Code
Installfest skill (ELO): use git on the command line, logged in to your GitHub account, to clone repos and push code
Interacting with Assignments: fork the assignment, work on it locally or in Codespaces, run its tests, then commit and push to your fork (no pull request needed)

steps.title: Install Docker Desktop and VS Code
steps.detail: Your CLAUDE.md already lists Docker and VS Code on this Mac, so this is a check, not a fresh install. In VS Code, open the command palette (Cmd+Shift+P) and run "Shell Command: Install 'code' command in PATH" so `code` works from any terminal.
steps.doneWhen: docker --version prints a version, and typing `code .` in a terminal opens that folder in VS Code.

steps.title: Install Homebrew and check its health
steps.detail: Homebrew is the Mac's package manager: it installs and updates developer tools for you. Install it from brew.sh if `brew` isn't found, then update it and run the health check.
steps.doneWhen: brew doctor says "Your system is ready to brew." Warnings are OK to read and skip for now.

steps.title: Install Python and a default venv
steps.detail: A virtual environment (venv) keeps each project's Python packages separate. Your CLAUDE.md lists Python 3.14, so just confirm it, then create and activate the default venv. Heads-up: the page creates `~/.default`, but its starter .zshrc line says `source $HOME/default/bin/activate` (no dot). Use the same name in both places or new terminals will show an error.
steps.code:
python3 --version
brew install python
cd ~
python3 -m venv .default
source ~/.default/bin/activate
steps.doneWhen: You see (.default) at the start of your prompt, and `deactivate` removes it.

steps.title: Install Node.js and npm
steps.detail: Node runs JavaScript outside the browser; npm installs JavaScript packages. Your CLAUDE.md lists Node 26, so the version checks are the important part.
steps.code:
brew install npm
sudo npm install -g n
sudo n stable
node -v
npm -v
steps.doneWhen: node -v and npm -v both print version numbers.

steps.title: Configure Git and log in to GitHub
steps.detail: Git saves snapshots of your code on your machine; GitHub stores them online. Use your GitHub username (cruzjay188) and the email on your GitHub account. You're already logged in to `gh` as cruzjay188, so the clone test just proves it works.
steps.code:
git config --global user.name "<YOUR_NAME>"
git config --global user.email "<YOUR_EMAIL>"
git config --global core.editor "code --wait"
git config --global -l
gh auth login
gh repo clone lodash/lodash
rm -rf lodash
steps.doneWhen: git config --global -l shows your user.name, user.email and core.editor=code --wait, and the lodash clone works.

steps.title: Install PostgreSQL and open psql
steps.detail: PostgreSQL is the database the course uses later (Supabase runs it in the cloud). Your CLAUDE.md doesn't list Postgres, so check whether you did this on Day 1.
steps.code:
brew install postgresql@14
brew services restart postgresql@14
psql postgres
steps.doneWhen: Your prompt changes to postgres=#. Type \q to leave.

steps.title: Add Live Server to VS Code
steps.detail: Every Knowledge Check is a team quiz you open with Live Server (right-click index.html → Open with Live Server). It's in the Installfest's recommended extensions, along with ESLint, Prettier, GitLens and others.
steps.doneWhen: Right-clicking an index.html in VS Code shows "Open with Live Server".

steps.title: Practice the command line (CLI Practice)
steps.detail: Do the Terminal Tutor course, then the README's exercise on your own Mac: make a test folder in ~, make test.txt with touch, edit it with `code`, view it with head/tail/less, go up a level and delete the folder. progress.md shows cli-practice as done, so use the README's "Points to Ponder" (cd ., cd .., cd ~, cd /, making, renaming and deleting files) as a self-quiz.
steps.doneWhen: You can answer every Points to Ponder question without looking it up.

steps.title: Learn the fork, clone, commit, push loop
steps.detail: Fork the assignment on GitHub (your own copy), clone your fork, work, then commit and push. In this workspace `/start-assignment` and `/save-project` do this for you, but know the manual commands too. Assignments aren't graded, and you submit by pushing.
steps.code:
git clone https://github.com/your-username/assignment-name.git
cd assignment-name
git status
git add .
git commit -m "Complete assignment section 1"
git push origin main
steps.doneWhen: Your commit shows on your fork's GitHub page (for example github.com/cruzjay188/cli-practice).

concepts.meaning: Typing text commands in a terminal instead of clicking around a window.
The family of operating systems macOS and Linux come from, which is why they share commands like ls and cd.
A tool that installs and updates software for you: brew for the Mac, pip for Python, npm for JavaScript.
A folder that holds one project's Python packages so projects don't clash.
A settings file your terminal runs every time it opens, used for PATH changes and aliases.
An absolute path starts from / (the top of the disk); a relative path starts from the folder you're in.
Your own copy of someone else's GitHub repo, under your account.
Downloading a GitHub repo to your computer.
A commit is a saved snapshot on your machine; a push uploads your commits to GitHub.
